questions.question: Which source-dataset mapping did the authors use when assembling BanStereoSet's categories?

options.A: StereoSet supplied race, gender, religion, profession; GenAssocBias supplied beauty, beauty-in-profession, ageism; IndiBias supplied caste; region was newly curated
options.B: IndiBias supplied race and gender; StereoSet supplied caste and region; GenAssocBias supplied religion and profession
options.C: StereoSet supplied all nine categories, while other datasets were used only for English evaluation
options.D: GenAssocBias supplied race, caste, and religion; all remaining categories were generated synthetically

questions.rationale: Section 2.1 states the category provenance, including the newly curated regional category.
questions.evidence_quote:
We derived our beauty, beauty in profes-
sion, and ageism bias categories from Kamruzza-
man et al.’s (2024b) bias detection dataset, here-
after referred to as the GenAssocBias dataset. The
caste bias category was adopted from the IndiBias
dataset (Sahoo et al., 2024). We freshly curated the
data for our regional bias category.

questions.question: How did the authors handle the lack of gendered pronouns in Bangla translations?

options.A: They inserted explicit phrases for 'a man' or 'a woman' in 76 sentences
options.B: They retained English pronouns in all 178 gender examples
options.C: They excluded gender examples because Bangla has no gender distinctions
options.D: They inferred gender from names in every sentence and changed 12 examples

questions.rationale: The translation subsection explains the pronoun ambiguity and says gender-specific phrases were added in 76 sentences.
questions.evidence_quote:
This modi-
fication was applied to 76 sentences.

questions.question: Which five StereoSet pitfalls did annotators explicitly address, and how many examples were affected by the 'incommensurable groups and attributes' issue?

options.A: Meaningful stereotype, misaligned stereotype, invalid perturbations, incommensurable groups/attributes, unnatural text; 58 cases
options.B: Gender ambiguity, name mismatch, regional mismatch, caste omission, and label imbalance; 76 cases
options.C: Meaningful stereotype, offensive language, mistranslation, label leakage, and duplication; 47 cases
options.D: Invalid perturbations, nonbinary exclusion, small categories, model fluency, and region coverage; 15 cases

questions.rationale: The authors list these five pitfalls and report counts 47, 9, 15, 58, and 35 respectively.
questions.evidence_quote: These pitfalls affected 47, 9, 15, 58, and 35 sentences of the ﬁnal dataset, respectively.

questions.question: What consensus rule governed retention of corrected StereoSet translations?

options.A: Keep a sentence only if at least three annotators agreed
options.B: Keep a sentence if any one annotator approved it
options.C: Require unanimous agreement from all four annotators
options.D: Retain sentences based on GPT-4 confidence alone

questions.rationale: The dataset construction states the minimum annotator agreement threshold after manual review and discussion.
questions.evidence_quote: We retained only sentences for which at least three annotators reached a consensus.

questions.question: How was newly curated regional-bias data generated before Bangla translation?

options.A: Start from 17 major Bangladeshi cities, ask ChatGPT for 10 stereotypical, 10 anti-stereotypical, and 10 unrelated attributes per city, then validate and create sentences with annotators
options.B: Translate 63 English region examples from StereoSet and preserve their original cities
options.C: Use 10 cities and one attribute per category, with no human validation
options.D: Ask annotators to write Bangla sentences first, then use ChatGPT to label stereotypes

questions.rationale: Section 2.5 details the city-based human-LLM workflow and the three sets of ten attributes per city.
questions.evidence_quote: We started with 17 major cities in Bangladesh

questions.question: Which category counts sum to the reported 1,194 examples in BanStereoSet?

options.A: Race 241, gender 178, religion 56, profession 206, ageism 134, beauty 130, beauty profession 126, caste 60, region 63
options.B: Race 206, gender 241, religion 60, profession 178, ageism 126, beauty 134, beauty profession 130, caste 56, region 63
options.C: Race 241, gender 178, religion 63, profession 206, ageism 130, beauty 134, beauty profession 126, caste 56, region 60
options.D: Race 178, gender 241, religion 56, profession 206, ageism 134, beauty 130, beauty profession 126, caste 60, region 63

questions.rationale: The paper gives these nine per-category counts; together they total 1,194.
questions.evidence_quote:
Each bias type in BanStereoSet con-
tains the following number of examples—Race:
241, Gender: 178, Religion: 56, Profession: 206,
Ageism: 134, Beauty: 130, Beauty Profession: 126,
Caste: 60, and Region: 63.

questions.question: What prompting and comparison setup underlies the main Bangla-versus-English model results?

options.A: Four multilingual LLMs; three Bangla prompting templates averaged, while English used modified English sentences and zero-shot evaluation
options.B: Four monolingual Bangla models; one prompt each, with few-shot English evaluation
options.C: GPT-4 only; three translated prompts in Bangla and five-shot prompts in English
options.D: Four models with human demonstrations in both languages and one shared unmodified English dataset

questions.rationale: The evaluation uses GPT-4o, Mistral-7B, llama3.1-70B, Gemma2-27B; Bangla scores average three prompts and English uses the modified English set zero-shot.
questions.evidence_quote: Following Gupta et al. (2023), we present our main results averaged across all three prompting templates.

questions.question: How should stereotypical-response rates be interpreted for categories derived from StereoSet, given the authors' stated desired behavior?

options.A: Prefer rates below 50% when stereotypic options encode extremely negative associations, rather than treating exact parity as ideal
options.B: Prefer exactly 50% for every category regardless of the stereotype's valence
options.C: Prefer 100% because unrelated responses are excluded from scoring
options.D: Prefer the highest rate in StereoSet categories and the lowest rate elsewhere

questions.rationale: They qualify the 50% parity target: extremely negative StereoSet stereotypes, such as terrorist associated with Afghanistan, should lead to lower stereotype selection.
questions.evidence_quote:
the desirable percent of stereo-
typical responses is lower than 50%. This stems
from the presence of extremely negative attributes
used for stereotypical associations in StereoSet,
such as stereotype linking ‘terrorist’ to Afghanistan

questions.question: What were the reported average stereotypical-response rates in Bangla for GPT-4o and Mistral, and how did they compare?

options.A: 73.78% for GPT-4o and 55.41% for Mistral, with Mistral lower
options.B: 55.41% for GPT-4o and 73.78% for Mistral, with GPT-4o lower
options.C: 69.73% for GPT-4o and 64.09% for Mistral, with a 5.64-point gap
options.D: 63.77% for GPT-4o and 59.94% for Mistral, from English results

questions.rationale: The Bangla Average row reports these values; the paper describes GPT-4o as more stereotypical on average and Mistral as least.

questions.question: Which limitations do the authors identify that specifically constrain generalization of BanStereoSet's bias measurements?

options.A: Regional stereotype variation may be underrepresented, gender is binary, some categories are small, and only explicit biases are captured
options.B: All categories have equal size, but the dataset contains only implicit bias and nonbinary examples
options.C: The dataset covers no religion or caste, and all examples are English-only
options.D: Human translation review was omitted, and the dataset includes only regional stereotypes

questions.rationale: The limitations section names regional representativeness, binary gender, small category sizes such as region, and omission of subtle/implicit bias among other caveats.
questions.evidence_quote:
the dataset may not adequately rep-
resent regional variations in stereotypes throughout
Bangladesh, as biases can vary markedly between
different areas. Moreover, the dataset’s focus on
binary gender (man and woman) representation re-
stricts its ability to address biases concerning non-
binary or gender-nonconforming identities.
